title: What a shared cache moved
subtitle: One claim, one hero number, and what it cost
thesis: Moving repeat work out of the request path changes latency first and everything else second.

evidence.label: Illustrative dataset for layout demonstration — not measured production data.
Instrumentation: server timings sampled at 10 percent

sections.heading: The claim
sections.summary: When a repeated lookup is served from cache, the request path does less work and every later change has to be reasoned about separately.
paragraphs: When a repeated lookup is served from cache, the request path does less work. The gain is easiest to see in latency, but the same move changes freshness, staleness and how a fix reaches readers.

sections.heading: Served from cache
sections.summary: In an illustrative quarter, 78 percent of lookups were served from cache instead of recomputed.

sections.heading: Before and after
sections.summary: The cache shortens the request path but introduces a freshness window that has to be owned.

sections.heading: Median lookup across the quarter
sections.summary: The median lookup fell week over week as more of the population ran against the cache.

chart.sourceNote: Illustrative dataset for layout demonstration — not measured production data.

sections.heading: Read with care
sections.summary: The latency figure is a median from sampled server timings, not a per-request measurement, and the sample misses the tail.
paragraphs: The latency figure is a median over sampled server timings, so it does not describe the slowest requests. The staleness that caching introduces is real and is reported separately rather than smoothed away.
